Giv (Persian: Gīv, also romanized Giv, Gīw) is one of the principal heroes (pahlavān) of the Persian epic tradition, best known from Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh. Below is a consolidated account of what classical sources (chiefly the Shahnameh) and later tradition record about him.

Identity and family
- Parentage and house: Giv is a member of the house (family) of Godarz—he is usually described as the son of Godarz, one of the great Iranian noblemen and champions. The House of Godarz is one of the important noble families in the epic, frequently serving the Kayanian kings.
- Children: In the Shahnameh Giv is the father of Bijan (also spelled Bizhan), another celebrated hero whose romance with Manijeh is one of the epic’s famous episodes. (Different later traditions sometimes supply more genealogical detail, but this father–son relationship is consistent in Ferdowsi.)
- Rank: He is repeatedly depicted as one of the foremost Iranian knights. In some enumerations of the “seven champions” or notable warriors of Iran in the epic he is counted among the top champions.

Character and attributes
- Reputation: Giv is presented as brave, steadfast, loyal to his king and Iran, reliable in councils of war, and respected by other chiefs (including Rostam and other great pahlavans). He is pious in the epic sense—loyal to the king and to the ideal of defending Iran.
- Role-type: He typically appears as a senior noble-warrior and counselor, not as the single superhuman slayer (like Rostam) but as a major actor whose leadership, counsel, and deeds are crucial to Iran’s fortunes.

Major episodes and deeds in the Shahnameh
(These are the best-known narrative moments; there are other appearances as the epic unfolds.)

- Service to Kay Kavus and Kay Khosrow: Giv is prominent in the reigns of the Kayanian kings Kay Kavus and especially Kay Khosrow. He fights in many campaigns against Turan and helps to re-establish Kayanian authority after periods of trouble.

- The search for Kay Khosrow: One of Giv’s most famous deeds is his role in finding and bringing Kay Khosrow to Iran. In the Shahnameh, Kay Kavus learns (or is told) of a young noble in Turan—Kay Khosrow, who is the son of Siyâvash (an Iranian prince) and Farangis (a Turanian princess). Kay Kavus sends a number of Iranian heroes to search for Kay Khosrow; Giv undertakes a long and difficult search. After searching for several years, he eventually locates Kay Khosrow and brings him back to Iran, where Kay Khosrow later becomes king. (This mission highlights Giv’s persistence and loyalty and is one of his defining narrative acts.)

- Wars with Turan and other campaigns: Giv appears in the large-scale Iranian–Turanian wars recounted in the Shahnameh. He is among the commanders and champions who fight against Turanian kings and chiefs. He takes part in the major battles of Kay Khosrow’s reign and in expeditions and ambushes described in the epic.

- Relationship with Rostam and other heroes: Giv acts alongside other great heroes—Rostam, Gorgin, Bizhan (his son), Roham, and others. He is on terms of mutual respect with Rostam: not a rival but a fellow champion whose counsel and prowess are relied upon.

- Later life and fate: Ferdowsi does not dwell on a sensational, separate death-story for Giv comparable to Rostam’s tragedy. Like many of the great noble heroes of the Shahnameh, Giv’s major legacy is his role in establishing Kay Khosrow’s rule and through his son Bijan. Different later traditions and regional tellings sometimes attach additional episodes or genealogical elaborations.

Name, language, and tradition
- Name and antiquity: The name Giv (Gīv) is an old Iranian personal name; forms of it and related names appear in Middle Persian (Pahlavi) and in some pre-Islamic lists of heroes. The figure in the Shahnameh draws on earlier epic and oral traditions that Ferdowsi incorporated and refined.
- Sources: The primary literary source for Giv’s life and deeds is Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh (completed c. 1010 CE). Elements of his character and stories appear in earlier Middle Persian and oral epic material that Ferdowsi used, and he is also present in later Persian commentaries, regional epic retellings, miniature painting cycles, and modern adaptations.

Cultural legacy
- Art and literature: Giv appears in Persian miniatures and manuscript illustrations of Shahnameh scenes—especially scenes of councils of heroes, the search for Kay Khosrow, and major battles. He is part of the web of tragic–heroic figures in Persian cultural memory.
- Modern references: Giv’s name and persona are sometimes invoked in modern Persian literature and popular culture when referring to courage, loyalty, and noble service.

Scholarly remarks and variant traditions
- Variations: As with many epic figures, the details of episodes and genealogies differ between manuscripts and later retellings. Some minor episodes associated with Giv in local tradition do not appear in the core Shahnameh narration; conversely, Ferdowsi may have condensed or reshaped older stories about him.
- Comparative notes: Scholars of Iranian epic note that Giv belongs to a class of noble warrior figures who function as loyal pillars of the heroic house (in Giv’s case, the house of Godarz). He contrasts with more solo-heroic types (Rostam) and with tragic or treacherous figures, representing dependable fealty to the throne.

If you want more detail on any of the following, I can provide it:
- A close, episode-by-episode retelling of Giv’s role in the search for Kay Khosrow (with chapter/line references from the Shahnameh).
- Passages where Giv speaks or is described (with translations).
- Visual and manuscript traditions showing Giv (examples of miniatures or museums).
- Comparative material from Middle Persian or other pre-Ferdowsi sources mentioning Giv.
